h1: A Google Business Profile for a taproom
title: Google Business Profile for a Taproom | Craft Beer School
desc: How to set up and manage a Google Business Profile for a taproom: verification, categories, hours, photos, posts, questions and reviews.
teaser: For a taproom the map listing is often the first thing a visitor sees. A complete, accurate profile costs nothing.
standfirst: A Google Business Profile is the free listing that appears on Google Search and Maps. For a taproom it is a shop window. Here is how to set it up and keep it honest.
sections:
When someone searches for a taproom or a bar nearby, results often show a map with a short list of places. The details shown come mostly from Business Profiles. People look at the photos, the rating, the hours and the phone number, often without ever opening a website.

We cannot promise where your listing will appear. Google decides, mainly on relevance, distance and prominence. What you can do is make your profile complete and accurate so it is a strong candidate.

Search for your venue on Google Maps and claim it, or create a new profile if none exists. Google will ask you to verify that you manage the business, by methods that depend on your country and may include a postcard, a phone call, an email or a video. Follow what is offered. Do not create duplicate profiles for the same place.

• Name: exactly your real-world business name. Adding keywords to the name breaks Google's rules and can lead to suspension.
  • Category: choose the main one that fits, then add secondary categories that are true, such as brewery or bar.
  • Address and area served: the same spelling as on your website.
  • Hours: including special hours for holidays. Wrong hours are the most common complaint.
  • Phone and website: a booking link where you have one.
  • Description: write plainly what you are, not a list of keywords.

Add real photos of the entrance, the room, the bar, the beer and the food. People use them to decide whether the place suits them. Use your own, in good light. Keep them current. Avoid images with heavy text.

Use posts to announce events, new beers and festive hours. Keep them short and accurate. Remember that alcohol content has rules on the platform. Local advertising rules apply too, so avoid anything that encourages heavy drinking or targets minors.

Where your listing lets visitors ask questions or send messages, check regularly and answer politely and accurately. Reply to reviews, good and bad, in a calm and brief way. We cover this in managing reviews and ratings for a brewery. Never buy reviews or ask staff to post them. Do not offer rewards for reviews, which the platform does not allow.
Keep it consistent with your website

The name, address and phone number should match across your Business Profile, website, social pages and listings. Differences confuse customers and weaken trust. Add the same details to your site's contact page in plain text. The wider site work is in SEO for breweries.

The most common is wrong hours. A visitor who arrives to a closed door writes a review about it. Next comes keyword stuffing in the name, which can get a profile suspended. Third is duplicates: two listings for the same place split reviews and confuse people.

Also watch for the profile of a closed or moved taproom. If you move, update the address rather than starting a new one, so reviews and history stay with you. If you close temporarily, mark it as such.

Finally, protect access. Use a business email with more than one trusted manager. Remove staff who leave. A profile locked to someone who has left can take a long time to recover. Keep a note of who manages it and how to reach them.

Review your profile each quarter with fresh eyes. Search for your taproom from a phone away from the venue and look at what a stranger sees: the first photo, the rating, the opening hours and the button to call. If anything looks wrong or out of date, fix it that day. Small repairs like these cost nothing and spare visitors a wasted trip.

If you run more than one outlet, create a separate profile for each location with its own address, phone number and hours.

Once a month: check the hours, add two or three new photos, post about any event, answer questions, reply to new reviews and look at the profile insights for searches and calls. It rarely takes more than an hour. Keep a note of what you change so that you can see what moves your numbers.
faqs: Is a Google Business Profile free?
Yes. Creating and managing a profile does not cost anything.
Can I show the beer menu?
Yes, you can add menu information or a link to your website. Keep it up to date, since an old menu disappoints visitors.
What if someone posts a false review?
You can report it for review by the platform. Reply politely in the meantime. Do not respond with accusations.
